strengths: Novel application of chaos theory (Lyapunov exponents, DFA) to discriminator design for speech bandwidth extension
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 1-2) systematically evaluating component contributions
Achieves parameter efficiency (33.5M parameters) with competitive or superior performance versus larger baselines
Multiple complementary objective evaluation metrics (6 metrics across fidelity, intelligibility, and perceptual quality)
Detailed experimental reporting including hyperparameters, dataset specifications, and hardware configuration
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Fundamental venue mismatch for ACL 2026—this is signal processing research without language processing components; better suited for ICASSP/Interspeech

Manuscript appears incomplete: Figures 2-3 labeled 'Dummy' without actual captions; subjective evaluation claimed in abstract but zero results shown; abstract lists MS-RD and MR-PPD not described anywhere in paper

Severely limited experimental validation: single dataset (VCTK, clean English only); no cross-dataset testing, noisy speech evaluation, or multilingual validation despite being essential for robustness claims

Weak theoretical justification: core hypothesis that discriminators capturing Lyapunov exponents improve reconstruction lacks rigorous mechanistic explanation; no empirical validation that these properties are actually captured

Marginal empirical improvements: NISQA-MOS gains over MS-BWE often <0.1 (4.24 vs 4.26); performance actually degrades for 2-48 kHz range (NISQA-MOS 3.9987) with no analysis; SI-SDR/SI-SNR similar or worse than baselines
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Table 3 has numerous 'NA' values; NU-Wave/EBEN/AERO results missing; cannot fairly assess claimed state-of-the-art status
Subjective evaluation claims unverifiable: abstract mentions 'five human judges' but paper provides no methodology, results, MOS scores, or inter-rater reliability

Missing critical implementation details: delay embedding parameters (d, τ) for MRLD unspecified; MSDFA tile size S undefined; adversarial loss weighting scheme never described; reproducibility severely compromised
Unclear contribution boundaries: paper conflates novel components (MRLD, MSDFA) with prior work (MRAD, MRPD acknowledged from Lu et al. 2024b); actual novelty contribution difficult to isolate
Presentation quality issues: dummy figures indicating incomplete work; grammatical errors; unexplained components (Schrodinger Bridge); Figure 1 caption uninformative; suggests rushed submission

strengths: Novel application of chaos theory (Lyapunov exponents, detrended fluctuation analysis) to speech bandwidth extension with clear scientific motivation
Significant parameter efficiency achieving 0.5x fewer parameters than AP-BWE (33.5M vs 72M) with better perceptual quality on NISQA-MOS, PESQ, and STOI metrics

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including 6 objective metrics, subjective MOS/pairwise preference tests, computational complexity analysis (MACs, FLOPs, RTF), and detailed ablation studies justifying design choices
Excellent reproducibility with extensive hyperparameter tables, dataset preprocessing details, architecture specifications, and inference workflows in appendices
Thorough technical presentation with dual-stream processing, Lattice-based stream interaction, and well-engineered generator architecture demonstrating solid engineering
weaknesses: Critically limited evaluation scope: tested only on VCTK (English, read speech) in noise-free settings with no cross-dataset, cross-lingual, or robustness evaluation—severely undermines generalizability claims and practical applicability

Unclear mechanism for chaos-based improvements: paper asserts Lyapunov exponents and DFA capture relevant features but provides no rigorous justification; ablation shows only +0.15 NISQA-MOS from adding MSDFA, suggesting incremental gains; missing analysis of what chaos discriminators actually learn differently

Missing critical technical details: delay-embedding parameters (d, τ) unspecified in Algorithm 1; unclear how Lyapunov exponents remain differentiable for backpropagation; DFA typically requires longer time series but used on 6-37ms windows; size S for tiling F(n) not specified

Limited novelty: applies classical techniques (Lyapunov exponents from 1968, DFA from 1994) to discriminators (incremental); ConformerNeXt is straightforward combination of Conformer and ConvNeXt; Lattice blocks from prior work; all loss functions are standard

Mixed performance on key metrics: SI-SDR and SI-SNR worsen compared to AP-BWE (13.24 vs 13.42 dB, 13.15 vs 13.35 dB); improvements primarily on NISQA-MOS (learned metric) and PESQ; modest 11% subjective preference with insufficient statistical validation

Weak subjective evaluation: only 10 participants (all Bangladeshi undergraduates, non-native English speakers), 30 samples per person, no confidence intervals or significance testing, 11% preference improvement over AP-BWE is marginal

Severe dataset limitations: VCTK contains read newspaper articles (not natural speech); limited to single language (English); no evaluation on noisy, reverberant, or realistic speech; only 110 speakers; no cross-speaker generalization analysis

Missing experimental rigor: no error bars or confidence intervals reported; no statistical significance testing between methods; no cross-validation; no analysis of failure cases; training time not compared with baselines; incomplete justification for loss weight selection (λ values appear arbitrary)
